title: The Global 100 Responds to the Big Four
pub: The Practice — Law Firm Responses to the Big Four
author: Robert J. Couture

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source addresses law firms’ strategic response to competition from the Big Four, especially inadequate threat assessment and the risks of operational and cultural transformation. It does not substantively assess AI-enabled legal workflows, verification, competence risks, bounded-task productivity or lawyer replacement, so its position on the cluster’s proposition cannot be determined.
qs: The most concerning observation is that a significant number of firms have given little or no thought to this competitive threat, and many of the interviewees expressed this concern.

Ignoring the question is also quite understandable because the actions driven by a conclusion of threat will require significant action, including the risks of making consequential operational and cultural changes.

st.t: Big Four: Integration matters more than replacement
st.an: Couture accepts integration rather than simple Big Four replacement as the central competitive dynamic and materially extends it with interview evidence identifying three law-firm responses: inaction, complementary partnerships, and law-firm-led multiprofessional delivery. He also specifies that full integration shifts coordination and sole contractual responsibility from the client to the law firm, while cautioning that no strategy is universally appropriate.
qs: These firms often will bring in the Big Four (or other capable consulting firms) to assist a client in larger projects that require process expertise, technology capabilities, or scale that the law firm cannot provide.

With an integrated solutions approach, the law firm is the organization with the sole contractual responsibility to deliver a solution and solve a problem, much like a general contractor on a construction project.

st.t: Provider convergence: Buyers coordinate an unbundled market
st.an: The source accepts that integrated, multidisciplinary delivery is expanding and materially extends the cluster by identifying its implications for lawyer careers and the strategic risks law firms face when partnering across provider boundaries. Its evidence is experiential and prospective, so it does not establish integrated providers’ superiority or displacement of incumbent firms.
qs: Working on a very large team of professionals in which the legal expertise is but one element of the services necessary to help the client—whether it is primarily a law firm, an accountancy, or a consulting firm—is an entirely different experience from the typical “big law” life.

Those pursuing a partnering strategy with other entities must take into consideration the risk of potentially subverting their client relationships by introducing new (and highly competent) strategic advisors to their clients, or perhaps losing some of their best professionals to enticing offers from their new business partners.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s operating-model emphasis and materially extends it by showing how competitive pressure can drive law firms toward integrated, multiprofessional delivery teams, new nonlawyer roles and redesigned partner capabilities. It does not assess AI’s jagged capabilities or verification directly, but provides a concrete organisational model for reallocating legal work rather than simply procuring technology.
qs: They plan to expand their professional practice offerings to better compete, which often means hiring billable professionals who are not lawyers to deliver integrated solutions.
These firms are adding new project managers, client managers, industry consultants, technology experts, and data scientists to build out a fully capable delivery team.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source accepts workflow segmentation and materially extends the synthesis by showing how incumbent law firms can rebundle multidisciplinary implementation work as prime contractors. It also supports the synthesis’s cautious view of uneven, pragmatic adaptation rather than rapid market-wide disruption.
qs: All the professionals and activities are procured, coordinated, and managed by the prime contractor (in this case, the law firm).
On these teams, lawyers’ time can often be 10 percent or less of the billable project work.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: Couture aligns with the cluster’s cautious, strategy-led account of operating-model change: firms should seriously assess provider-side competitive threats and the operational and cultural consequences of responding, rather than assume transformation is automatic or universally required. His evidence is about the Big Four rather than AI specifically, so it supports the cluster’s broader competitive and organisational logic without substantiating AI-driven bargaining shifts directly.
qs: The most concerning observation is that a significant number of firms have given little or no thought to this competitive threat, and many of the interviewees expressed this concern.
Serious critical thinking that analyzes the situation and concludes that no changes are necessary based on their strategic analysis is admirable.

kp.k: Big Four expansion challenges established legal-market positions
kp.d: This 2021 article examines competition and multiprofessional delivery rather than AI specifically. Couture reports that the Big Four had developed law practices in more than 85 countries with more than 10,000 attorneys, receiving recognition from major ranking services. He frames this expansion as a potential threat to law firms whose markets have historically enjoyed regulatory protection.
qs: While the Big Four (or Big Five) have been threatening entry into the legal market since the late ’90s, they have been quietly adding capability, which now places their law practices in more than 85 countries with a legal workforce of more than 10,000 attorneys.

kp.k: Interview evidence identifies three strategic responses
kp.d: Couture conducted in-depth interviews with leadership at 20 Global 100 firms from January through October 2020, including global chairs, managing partners, chief operating officers and heads of global strategy. The resulting strategies were maintaining existing operations, establishing complementary Big Four relationships, and transforming into integrated multiprofessional providers. He describes the sample as fairly representative but explicitly cautions that interviewing 20 different firms could yield different findings.
qs: I conducted in-depth interviews with leadership of Global 100 firms from January through October 2020
The firms interviewed are largely pursuing three fundamental strategies:
Interviews with 20 different firms could yield a different story

kp.k: Competitive awareness and business-loss reporting were limited
kp.d: Little more than a third of interviewees had high familiarity with Big Four activity, just less than half were casually aware, and less than a quarter had virtually no knowledge. Half perceived competition as current, while the other half placed any impact more than five years ahead. About a third reported experiencing competition; half did not know whether they had lost business because partners did not report competitive losses. These are reported perceptions and reporting limitations, not measured market-share effects.
qs: Half of the firms observed that competition from the Big Four was here today, and the other half believed that any impact would be more than five years in the future.
About a third of the firms in the sample have already experienced Big Four competition, but the majority did not have recent experience.
half of the firms didn’t know if they had lost business because their partners don’t report competitive losses, even if they are locally known.

kp.k: Exposure varied by geography and practice area
kp.d: Most competitive reporting concerned Europe, followed by Asia/Pacific. Tax was the most targeted practice, followed by compliance, regulatory, immigration and general corporate work including M&A. Firms with offices in more than 10 countries were most likely to take concrete competitive action; the majority operating in 10 countries or fewer took none.
qs: Often the experience with Big Four competition is different in each geographic region, with the majority of competitive reporting coming from Europe.
Asia/Pacific was the second most mentioned region.
the most targeted practice by the Big Four was quite understandably the tax practice, followed by compliance, regulatory, immigration, and general corporate work including M&A.

kp.k: Revenue per lawyer provides an imperfect segmentation proxy
kp.d: Couture segments firms by countries with offices and revenue per lawyer (RPL), treating RPL as a proxy for work sophistication while acknowledging productivity and regional pricing differences. The 2020 Global 100 average was approximately $975,000. Illustrative extremes were Wachtell at $3.3M and one country, and Dentons at $264,000 and 78 countries; these examples illustrate the market range without identifying interview participants.
qs: Of course, this is not a perfect measure, and differences in productivity and geographic regional pricing will impact this number
For reference, the average RPL in the 2020 Global 100 report is approximately $975,000.

kp.k: Inaction reflected both deliberate positioning and neglected analysis
kp.d: The majority interviewed made no operational changes because of Big Four competition; more than three-quarters of that group had locations in 10 countries or fewer. Some had carefully concluded that their work was insulated from near-term competition, while others had undertaken little or no analysis. Interviewees expressed both confidence in moving upstream or regulatory protection and concern about shallow awareness or weaker relationships outside legal departments.
qs: The majority of the firms interviewed have chosen to make no changes in their operation due to Big Four presence or competition.
In other cases, little or no analysis has been done and firms are ignoring the threat of new competition, although some of the interviewees expressed concern over the lack of critical assessment.
We are moving upstream, so we shouldn’t see any competition from them.
Our awareness is 1-inch deep.

kp.k: High-end global firms pursued complementary Big Four relationships
kp.d: Every interviewed firm adopting this strategy had offices in more than 10 countries and RPL above $975,000, although not all firms within those boundaries adopted it. These firms typically handled sophisticated, high-stakes work and brought in consultants for process expertise, technology or scale they could not supply internally. Their approach depended on trust that providers would respect client relationships and differentiated expertise; one interviewee described law-firm GC relationships as a resource the Big Four lacked.
qs: These firms often will bring in the Big Four (or other capable consulting firms) to assist a client in larger projects that require process expertise, technology capabilities, or scale that the law firm cannot provide.
All the firms interviewed that have chosen this strategic approach have offices in more than 10 countries and RPL greater than the Global 100 average of $975,000
The Big Four are worried about not having a good relationship with the GC, and we can remedy that deficiency.

kp.k: Integrated delivery makes firms responsible for complete solutions
kp.d: Broadly international firms with typically lower RPL and routine operational work were expanding into integrated professional services. Couture distinguishes integration from merely offering multiple disciplines: the law firm assumes sole contractual responsibility for the solution and coordinates all professionals, rather than leaving the client to integrate their contributions. Lawyers’ time could represent 10 percent or less of billable project work. The model lets firms retain downstream implementation work arising from their initial advice.
qs: With an integrated solutions approach, the law firm is the organization with the sole contractual responsibility to deliver a solution and solve a problem, much like a general contractor on a construction project.
On these teams, lawyers’ time can often be 10 percent or less of the billable project work.
This contrasts with a more typical approach where the law firm may work with other professionals, but the client is the systems integrator.

kp.k: Integrated models diversify roles and required partner capabilities
kp.d: Transforming firms were adding billable nonlawyer professionals, including project managers, client managers, industry consultants, technology experts and data scientists, and recruiting from the Big Four and other consultancies. Project management, client management and solution selling became important partner skills. Integrated engagements also opened relationships with operational business executives outside corporate legal departments.
qs: These firms are adding new project managers, client managers, industry consultants, technology experts, and data scientists to build out a fully capable delivery team.
These firms are also hiring from the Big Four and other consultancies to immediately gain access to the unique skills required for successful delivery in this model.

Many of these firms also recognize that new partner skills are required to deliver integrated practice offerings and have identified project management, client management, and solution selling as critical skills for successful partners when offering an integrated solutions approach.

kp.d: Interviewees offered contrasting views of regulatory protection: one regarded the ABA as a defensive barrier, while another argued that Rule 5.4 prevented firms from learning to compete with integrated providers. A transforming-firm interviewee said nonlawyer partners were needed. These are attributed strategic opinions, not findings about the rule’s legal effects or evidence of regulatory change.
qs: We have a moat around our castle via the ABA.

In the United States, the ABA is not doing law firms any favors with Rule 5.4 because they are not learning how to compete with integrated solutions being offered by the Big Four and other consultancies.
We need partners who are not lawyers to compete.

kp.k: Client demand independently motivated integrated service expansion
kp.d: A separate group of high-RPL firms with limited geographic footprints built integrated multiprofessional teams for client needs and business opportunities rather than as a response to the Big Four. They generally began in a focused practice or industry where they already had expertise, pursued global delivery, and expected expansion into other practices. Couture describes these as substantive service expansions rather than pilots.
qs: One additional strategic approach had nothing to do with the Big Four entering the legal marketplace.

These firms, with a high RPL and operating in a limited global footprint, have decided to build fully integrated, multiprofessional delivery teams because they sensed a client need combined with a business opportunity.
At this point these are not intended to be pilots but an expansion of their ability to provide clients a more complete set of professional services with multiple practices.

kp.k: Multiprofessional teams may alter lawyers' careers and development
kp.d: Couture argues that integrated delivery could produce substantially different careers from conventional large-firm practice. A former senior law-firm partner working at a Big Four firm reported broader expertise, more client contact, institutionalized teamwork and mentoring, and greater apparent upward mobility because partners retired earlier. Couture suggests revenue-oriented rather than hours-and-rates objectives may explain some satisfaction, while explicitly warning that this positive individual experience is not universal.
qs: The teamwork is much more institutionalized, significantly helping out the younger professionals because they aren’t reliant on one or two partners for their mentoring.
Also, upward mobility seems greater because the partners retire much earlier than in law firms, opening up opportunities for rising stars.
Not everyone will have such a delightful experience, but there is no question that the environment and opportunities could be very different as this delivery model of integrated solutions expands.

kp.k: All strategies require contingency planning and adaptation
kp.d: Couture identifies prospective risks rather than demonstrated outcomes: collaboration may weaken client relationships or facilitate talent losses; integrated transformation may demand underestimated technical and cultural effort; inaction may underestimate new competitors. He recommends testing assumptions, preparing implementable alternatives and maintaining the ability to change rapidly. His principal concern is that a significant number of firms had given the competitive threat little or no thought, not that every firm must transform.
qs: Those pursuing a partnering strategy with other entities must take into consideration the risk of potentially subverting their client relationships by introducing new (and highly competent) strategic advisors to their clients, or perhaps losing some of their best professionals to enticing offers from their new business partners.
Contingency plans must be in place and readily implementable.
The most concerning observation is that a significant number of firms have given little or no thought to this competitive threat
Serious critical thinking that analyzes the situation and concludes that no changes are necessary based on their strategic analysis is admirable.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The article makes no concrete claims or predictions about AI changing legal services.
pts.d: Couture examines Global 100 firms’ responses to Big Four competition and the growth of integrated, multiprofessional services. References to technology capabilities, technology experts and data scientists do not explicitly concern AI and should not be treated as AI claims. The AI-related titles appended after the article are links or event listings, not substantive claims from this source. This is a legal-market source rather than a cross-domain source.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: No evidence is offered about AI’s effects; the research evidence concerns competitive strategy.
pts.d: The author’s interviews with leaders of 20 Global 100 firms support the article’s account of responses to Big Four entry, not findings about AI adoption or impact.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: No AI-specific timeframe or conditions are stated.
pts.d: The article was published in March/April 2021 and draws on interviews conducted in January–October 2020. Its distinctions between competition already occurring and impacts expected more than five years later refer to the Big Four, not AI.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: No group is identified as affected specifically by AI.
pts.d: The article discusses effects of Big Four competition and integrated service delivery on Global 100 firms, lawyers, other professionals and corporate clients. It does not attribute those effects to AI.
